note: CROSS-KIT AGREEMENT VECTORS — the one input both language kits are run against, so a concept present in more than one kit is proven to MEAN the same thing rather than merely share a name. Consumed by scripts/graph-cross-kit.mjs, which transpiles and evaluates the TypeScript node and compiles and runs the Rust node against the same cases. Add a case here, not in the runner: the runner is the mechanism, this is the contract.
missConvention: A search that finds nothing is -1 here. TypeScript returns -1 directly; Rust returns Option::None and the runner maps None to -1. That mapping is a DECLARED convention, not an accident — if a kit ever returns something else, the run must fail rather than be normalised into agreement.

concepts.note: The two kits implement DIFFERENT quicksorts — Rust partitions functionally around xs[0] and returns a new Vec, TypeScript does an in-place Lomuto partition around the last element. Their traces and step counts differ; only the RESULT is contracted here, which is exactly why an output-level vector is the right instrument for this pair.

notComparable.note: Concepts present in both kits that this vector deliberately does NOT cover, and why. Recorded so the gap is a decision rather than an oversight.

graph.reason: The kits take incompatible inputs: Rust takes an adjacency HashMap<String, Vec<(String, u32)>>, TypeScript takes separate nodes[] and edges[] arrays. Comparing them needs an adapter that is itself a third representation of the graph, and that adapter would have to be trusted. Worth doing, but as its own decision.

falseMatch.reason: NOT the same concept. rotate.rs rotates a 3-D vector about an axis by an angle; rotate90.ts rotates a matrix by 90 degrees. They collide only under name normalisation, and contracting them together would assert an agreement that is meaningless.
